source_text: Ἀνεμνήσθη καὶ τῆς τρα πέζης ἐκείνης τῶν τριῶν παίδων, οἳ νέοι ληφθέντες, καὶ πάσης ἔρημοι προστασίας ὄντες, ἐν ἀλλοτρίᾳ γῇ καὶ βαρβάρῳ χώρᾳ τοσαύτην ἐπεδείξαντο φιλοσο φίαν, ὡς μέχρι νῦν ᾄδεσθαι τὴν ἀνδρείαν αὐτῶν. Καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ τὴν οἰκείαν ἔχοντες γῆν ἠσέβησαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ ναῷ διατρίβοντες εἰδωλολάτρουν· οἱ δὲ νέοι ἐκεῖνοι εἰς τὴν βαρβαρικὴν ἀπενεχθέντες γῆν, ἔνθα εἴδωλα καὶ πάσης ἀσεβείας ὑπόθεσις, τὴν πατρῴαν διετέλεσαν φυλάττοντες πολιτείαν. Εἰ τοίνυν οἱ αἰχμάλωτοι, καὶ δοῦλοι, καὶ νέοι πρὸ τῆς χάριτος τοσαύτην ἐπεδείξαντο φιλοσοφίαν, φησὶ, ποίας ἂν εἴημεν ἡμεῖς συγγνώμης ἄξιοι, μηδὲ πρὸς τὴν αὐτὴν ἐκείνοις ἀρετὴν φθάσαι δυνηθέντες; γʹ. Ταῦτα δὴ πάντα λογιζόμενος κατεγέλα τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου πονηρίας, κατεφρόνει τῆς κακουργίας, καὶ πρὸς οὐδὲν ἐνεδίδου τῶν ὁρωμένων. Ὡς δ' οὖν εἶδεν οὐδὲν αὐτῷ τι πλέον γενόμενον ὁ μιαρὸς ἐκεῖνος, ἄγει πάλιν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον, καὶ βασανίζων συνεχεῖς ἐπῆγε πεύσεις· ὁ δὲ πρὸς ἑκά στην πεῦσιν ἀπεκρίνατο, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι, μόνον. καὶ λέγοντος τοῦ δημίου· Ποίας εἶ πατρίδος; Χριστιανός εἰμι, φησί· Τί ἔχεις ἐπιτήδευμα; Χριστιανός εἰμι· Τίνας προγόνους; ὁ δὲ πρὸς ἅπαντα ἔλεγεν, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι· ἑνὶ τούτῳ καὶ ψιλῷ τῷ ῥήματι τοῦ διαβόλου πλήττων τὴν κεφαλὴν, καὶ συνεχῆ καὶ ἐπάλληλα τὰ τραύματα αὐτῷ παρέχων. Καίτοι γε καὶ τῆς ἔξωθεν παιδεύσεως μετέσχεν, ἀλλ' ᾔδει σαφῶς ὅτι ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀγῶσιν οὐ ῥητορείας χρεία, ἀλλὰ πίστεως· οὐ δεινότητος λόγου, ἀλλὰ φιλοθέου ψυχῆς· ἀρκεῖ ῥῆμα ἓν, φησὶν, ἅπασαν τοῦ διαβόλου τρέψαι τὴν φάλαγγα. Καὶ δοκεῖ μὲν τοῖς οὐκ ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάζουσιν ἀνακόλουθος εἶναι ἡ ἀπόκρισις· εἰ δέ τις τὸν νοῦν ἐπιστήσειε, καὶ ἐκ ταύτης ὄψεται τοῦ μάρτυρος τὴν σοφίαν. Ὁ γὰρ εἰπὼν, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι, καὶ πατρίδα, καὶ γένος, καὶ ἐπιτήδευμα, καὶ πάντα ἐδήλωσε· πῶς, ἐγὼ λέγω· Ὁ Χριστιανὸς οὐκ ἔχει πόλιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἄνω Ἱερουσαλήμ· Ἡ γὰρ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ, φησὶν, ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν, ἥτις ἐστὶ μήτηρ ἡμῶν. Ὁ Χριστιανὸς οὐκ ἔχει γήϊνον ἐπιτήδευμα, ἀλλ' εἰς τὴν ἄνω πολιτείαν τελεῖ· Ἡμῶν γὰρ, φησὶ, τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει· ὁ Χριστιανὸς συγγενεῖς ἔχει τοὺς ἁγίους ἅπαντας καὶ συμπολίτας· Συμπολῖται γάρ ἐσμεν τῶν ἁγίων, φησὶ, καὶ οἰκεῖοι τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ὥστε ἑνὶ ῥήματι, καὶ τίς εἴη, καὶ πόθεν, καὶ τίνων, καὶ τί πράττων διατελοίη, μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἐδίδαξε. Καὶ μετὰ ταύτης τῆς φωνῆς τὸν βίον κατέλυσε, καὶ ἀπῆλθε σώαν τῷ Χριστῷ τὴν παρακαταθήκην κομίζων, καὶ τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα δι' ὧν ἔπαθε παραινῶν ἐνίστασθαι, καὶ μηδὲν δεδοικέναι, ἀλλ' ἢ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ ἄρνησιν μόνον. Ταῦτ' οὖν καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰδότες ἐν καιρῷ τῆς εἰρήνης τὰ τοῦ πολέμου μελετῶμεν, ἵν' ἐπιστάντος τοῦ πολέμου λαμπρὸν καὶ ἡμεῖς στήσωμεν τρόπαιον. Κατεφρόνησεν ἐκεῖνος λιμοῦ, καταφρονήσωμεν καὶ ἡμεῖς τρυφῆς, καὶ τῆς γαστρὸς τὴν τυραννίδα καθέλωμεν, ἵνα ἂν καιρὸς ἐπιστῇ τοσαύτην παρ' ἡμῶν τὴν ἀν δρείαν ἐπιζητῶν, προγυμνασθέντες ἐν τοῖς ἐλάττοσι, λαμπροὶ φανῶμεν ἐπὶ τῶν σκαμμάτων. Ἐπὶ ἀρχόντων καὶ βασιλέων ἐπαῤῥησιάσατο ἐκεῖνος· τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς ποιῶμεν νῦν, κἂν ἐν συλλόγοις Ἑλλήνων πλουτούντων καὶ περιφανῶν συνεδρεύωμεν, μετὰ παῤῥησίας τὴν πίστιν ὁμολογῶμεν· καταγελῶμεν τῆς ἐκείνων πλάνης.
thought_title: Lucian's one-word confession and its meaning
orientation: Chrysostom is describing how Lucian, after enduring starvation and the sight of idol-food, was brought again to trial and answered every question only with 'I am a Christian.'
pass_a_gloss: He remembered also that table of the three youths, who, taken young, and being bereft of all protection, in a foreign land and barbarous country displayed so great self-discipline, that until now their courage is sung. And the Jews, even having their own land, acted impiously, and while spending time in the temple they worshipped idols; but those youths, carried off into the barbarian land, where idols and the occasion of every impiety were, continued guarding the ancestral citizenship. If therefore the captives, and slaves, and youths before grace displayed so great self-discipline, he says, of what pardon would we be worthy, if we were not able even to reach the same virtue as those? 3. Reckoning all these things, he laughed at the wickedness of the devil, he despised the malice, and he yielded to none of the things seen. When therefore that abominable one saw that nothing more was coming to him, he brings him again into the court, and torturing him he put forward continuous questions; but he answered to each question, that I am a Christian, only. And when the executioner said: Of what fatherland are you? I am a Christian, he says; What occupation do you have? I am a Christian; What ancestors? and he said to all things, that I am a Christian; with this one and bare word striking the head of the devil, and providing continuous and repeated wounds to him. And yet he had shared also in outside education, but he knew clearly that in such contests there is need not of rhetoric, but of faith; not of cleverness of speech, but of a God-loving soul; one word is enough, he says, to turn the whole phalanx of the devil. And the answer seems to those who do not examine carefully to be inconsistent; but if someone should fix his mind, he will see from this also the wisdom of the martyr. For the one who said, that I am a Christian, indicated both fatherland, and family, and occupation, and everything; how, I say: The Christian does not have a city on the earth, but the heavenly Jerusalem; For the heavenly Jerusalem, he says, is free, which is our mother. The Christian does not have an earthly occupation, but he belongs to the heavenly citizenship; For our citizenship, he says, exists in heaven; the Christian has as relatives all the saints and fellow-citizens; For we are fellow-citizens of the saints, he says, and members of the household of God. So with one word, both who he might be, and whence, and of what family, and what he continued doing, he taught with precision. And with this voice he ended his life, and departed bringing the deposit safe to Christ, and by what he suffered exhorting those after these things to stand firm, and to fear nothing, except sin and denial only. Knowing these things therefore, let us also in time of peace practice the things of war, so that when war stands upon us we too may set up a shining trophy. That one despised starvation; let us also despise luxury, and let us tear down the tyranny of the belly, so that if a time should stand upon us demanding such courage from us, having trained beforehand in smaller things, we may appear shining in the arenas. Before rulers and kings that one spoke boldly; let us also do this now, even if we sit in gatherings of rich and distinguished Greeks, let us confess the faith with boldness; let us laugh at their error.

pass_b_english: He also remembered the table of those three young men, who were taken as youths and had no one to protect them, yet in a foreign and barbarous land showed such self-discipline that their courage is sung about even to this day. The Jews, who had their own land, acted impiously, and even while spending their time in the temple they worshipped idols; but those young men, carried off into a barbarous land where idols and every occasion for impiety surrounded them, kept guarding their ancestral way of life to the end. If captives, slaves, and youths before the time of grace showed such self-discipline, he said, what pardon could we possibly deserve if we cannot even reach the same virtue they had?

Reasoning through all these things, he laughed at the devil's wickedness, despised his malice, and yielded to none of the things he saw. When that foul one saw that he was gaining nothing more, he brought him again to the tribunal, and while torturing him he kept putting forward question after question. But to each question Lucian answered only, 'I am a Christian.' And when the executioner said, 'What is your homeland?' he said, 'I am a Christian.' 'What is your occupation?' 'I am a Christian.' 'Who are your ancestors?' To everything he answered, 'I am a Christian,' striking the devil's head with this one bare phrase and dealing him wound after wound in rapid succession.

He had in fact received a secular education, but he knew clearly that in contests like these what is needed is not rhetoric but faith, not cleverness of speech but a soul that loves God. One phrase is enough, he said, to turn back the whole phalanx of the devil. To those who do not examine carefully, the answer seems irrelevant; but if someone pays attention to its meaning, he will see the martyr's wisdom even in this. For by saying 'I am a Christian,' he revealed his homeland, his family, his occupation, and everything. How? I will tell you. A Christian has no city on earth, but the heavenly Jerusalem. For the heavenly Jerusalem is free, and she is our mother (Galatians 4:26). A Christian has no earthly occupation, but fulfills the way of life above. For our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). A Christian has all the saints as relatives and fellow citizens. For we are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household (Ephesians 2:19). So with one phrase he taught with precision who he was, where he came from, who his people were, and what he continued to do.

And with this confession he ended his life, and departed carrying the deposit safe to Christ, and by what he suffered he urged those who came after to stand firm and fear nothing except sin and denial alone. Since we know these things, let us train in time of peace for the things of war, so that when war comes we too may set up a shining trophy. He despised starvation; let us also despise luxury, and let us tear down the tyranny of the belly, so that if a time comes demanding such courage from us, having trained beforehand in smaller things, we may appear radiant in the arenas. He spoke boldly before rulers and kings; let us do the same now. Even if we sit in gatherings of rich and prominent Greeks, let us confess the faith with boldness; let us laugh at their error.
